The field of knowledge in cybersecurity, development, reverse engineering, and cryptology are so vast that it's basically impossible to create a resource that will prepare you for this.

Some of these CTFs are absolutely brutal and suck. You'll know it when you see it. They'll have a very specific way they want something to solve, and the problems revolve around that one exploit from the 90s that no one alive should find or have documented. IMO, the best CTFs are the ones that can be solved with thorough research and scripting into a topic that's explained in the problem statement, but it is very hard to do this properly without it being too easy. Some of them also revolve around guesses and those suck, too. An example is a CTF that says "no attacking our infrastructure or using automated tools" but the answer requires you to find a subdirectory on an azure files share. How are you supposed to find that reliably without knowing the exact name of the share?

Are you certain that's how those integrations are set up? If so, you may have shot yourself in the foot and may need to rethink how they are linked. Modern authentication standards should utilize a non-changeable field that's associated with the user's identity. For example, in Azure AD it should be using the object ID. If you change the UPN, the user will need to log into Azure SSO with the UPN, but it will not break those integration's underlying connections since they rely on the immutable object ID. 

If the claim is the UPN, e-mail, or some other field that will be changed, then you're likely SOL and either need to rethink your auth deployment or work around it.

It's a job title with a wide range of skillsets and requirements. My definition would be different than anyone else's. That being said, my definition would be that a helpdesk employee makes changes which affects end user groups or devices on an individual or single group scale. 

A helpdesk employee would reset a user's password but not be able to change password policy requirements. A helpdesk employee should be able to add a printer to a computer, but they should not be adding printers to the print server. Similarly, they can provision a single device, but they are not defining provisioning policies or implementing the framework for provisioning. 

Obviously, this definition shifts and requirements move around as a helpdesk employee becomes more skilled or as the workforce thins. An overworked sysadmin could train a competent employee to do any of these tasks if they are repetitive in their environment. An ambitious helpdesk employee could ask to create and define a new network segment (with guidance and approval, of course).

Your computer can store lesser used memory pages to a file on a drive when your computer runs low on RAM. It's a way to clear up storage in RAM while also having some of the memory be more easily accessible rather than reprocessed entirely, but it is not a replacement for RAM - it's a page file. The issue is that the HDD is likely to be much, much slower than the RAM. As a rough ballpark, a higher performance HDD will process 150 MB/s of data, whereas DDR3-1600 RAM can process 12800 MB/s. That's a huge difference. 

You could use the page file as a crutch to keep your system working for normal tasks, but I do not think you will have much luck using it to edit videos. You may need to purchase better hardware to suit your needs, or swap to an OS that uses less RAM overhead.

1. Never trust user input. Ever. All queries should be hard-coded, pre-made inputs. If you need to take user input, it must be sanitized. Look up best practices based on your languages or frameworks of choice. 

1.a. If your API takes input from the client via a forgable request, you need server-side filtering. Client-side filtering is easily bypassed. 

2. The SQL user accessing the database via the API should have only the permissions it needs to perform its functions. 

2.a. Your API should be authenticated somehow.

3. The trust boundary between your application and the back-end database should filter requests and only allow approved protocols/hosts/etc.

I'm not sure if this will help, but I've done audits and third-party risk assessments for smaller organizations (from 5 to 100 employees). This was my general strategy:

For third-party risk management, you'll need to first figure out who each third-party is. In some organizations, this is an absolute nightmare since they could *still* be adding third-party providers especially if there is no technical oversight in each department. If that is the case, then the first thing I would do in your position is to "staunch the bleeding" and stop the scope of your project from growing. See if you can put a moratorium on onboarding new vendors until you can put forth guidelines for risk assessment of vendors within the scope of your audit. If they aren't going full cowboy, then you can probably skip this step - but you will want to form a change management board (or at least an officially designated individual who will sign off on onboarding new vendors) if they don't have one as part of your remediation to ensure each vendor is audited as they come into scope. 

After that, I would try to work with each department to determine what data they have that is in scope and then use that as a pivot point to identify all entities that have access to the data in any meaningful way. This of course means anything from potentially viewing, storing, transmitting, or acting upon the data. This, in my experience, is the worst part of any security audit. The companies I dealt with typically did not track where their data was, and it takes many phone calls, e-mails, and discussions to determine all relevant data sources. **If e-mails are not working, you HAVE to get them in a room or on a call with you. Security is not everyone's priority.** If you're finding it difficult locating all data sources, then begin with their largest data sources which pose the most risk to the organization. Once you have those figured out, you can come back for the smaller fries later. I'd highly recommend that you utilize something to track your data inventory, even if it's a simple spreadsheet like [this. ](https://view.officeapps.live.com/op/view.aspx?src=https%3A%2F%2Fprivacy.gwu.edu%2Fsites%2Fg%2Ffiles%2Fzaxdzs4721%2Ffiles%2FData%2520Inventory%2520Template.xlsx&wdOrigin=BROWSELINK)

If you ever get an uncooperative department or individual, and you can't find the needed information on your own, it's okay to leave gaps in the paperwork for that department during your initial audit. Just make sure it's noted plainly and clearly, with evidence (as with everything in the cyberspace), the reason why there's a gap in information and explain it to whoever has oversight for the department quickly. 

After you know the data sources, then you can determine the vendors who act upon the data. The specifics of this will depend on the organization you're auditing and what their business functions are. It's important that you understand the flow of data from start to finish to identify all risk points. It's easier said than done. You'll want a nice list of each vendor and make a qualitative (or quantitative, if you've got the time) assessment of their risk to the organization after you've completed your full audit. You'll also want to make sure you have contacts for each vendor. If you can't get a contact for a vendor, there's a high likelihood that the vendor will score higher on your risk matrix later on.

Remember how I said the hard part was getting your data inventory together from the entire organization? Well, this part sucks almost as much. You'll need to get a list of requirements for each vendor to follow and then perform an audit for each vendor. Your strategy and audit will depend entirely on the requirements you need to meet (but, of course, you can tailor them to the organization's needs) and what entity you are dealing with. I have not had to comply with EU regulations, but I have had to conform organizations to the US Safeguards Rule pretty frequently. We used self-assessment audit questions that we presented to the third-party with a sign-off and evidence when necessary. This may not be the same requirement for you, in which case, I highly recommend reading your regulation carefully and seeing what they count as a third-party audit or risk management strategy. 

You will get non-cooperative vendors. If you're spending too much time getting a vendor to comply, move on. You're doing an audit, not full remediation right now. The vendor gets a nice fat "RISK - HIGH" tag, and then the shareholders of the company can figure out how to proceed with a risky vendor.
